## Overview

The Bashkirs (Bashkir *Başqorttar*) are a Turkic people indigenous to Russia, concentrated in the republic of Bashkortostan and in the wider historical region of Badzhgard, which straddles both flanks of the Ural Mountains where Eastern Europe meets North Asia. Smaller communities live in Tatarstan, Perm Krai and the Chelyabinsk, Orenburg, Tyumen, Sverdlovsk and Kurgan oblasts, with a sizeable minority in Kazakhstan. The 2021 Russian census recorded 1,571,879 Bashkirs, of whom 1,268,806 — 31.5% of the republic's population — live in Bashkortostan. Their language belongs to the Kipchak branch of Turkic. In folk-culture terms the Bashkirs matter as a formerly half-nomadic people of the Ural steppe and mountain pastures whose herding, horse-based diet, wild-hive beekeeping and Tengrist-rooted epic poetry survived into the written record, and whose museum-held material culture is dominated by archery gear, felt and linen dress, and turned and carved wooden vessels.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used here document Bashkir textiles chiefly through the catalogued garments rather than through named weaving or printing traditions, so only what those records describe is given.

**Embroidered linen shirt** — A man's shirt of natural cream tabby linen, cut from a single full loom width (about 39 cm) at centre front and back with a further full width at each side and four added panels, producing an A-line body; sleeves are set in at right angles over large diamond-shaped gussets of red tabby linen. The slit neckline is faced inside with a linen panel and trimmed outside with applied red tabby cotton.

**Felted men's headwear** — A domed man's hat with points at either side, built from several pieces of cream-grey coarse felted cloth and hand stitched, its bottom edge bound with dark red tabby cotton. The combination of coarse undyed felt with a contrasting red cotton binding is the distinguishing treatment in the catalogued examples.

**Motif vocabulary.** The one motif the sources name is a symmetrical stylized leaf, embroidered in outline on the shirt; the decorative contrast of red cotton or linen against undyed cream cloth runs through both the shirt and the hat.

### Clothing & dress

For dress the sources are limited to the three catalogued garments and to what the written sources say about livelihood, so the picture is partial. Men's dress is represented by the cream tabby linen shirt described above, whose neckline is further decorated with white and green glass beads grouped in threes, with a single group of yellow; by the domed, side-pointed felt hat edged in dark red cotton; and by boots made of leather and horse skin. Horse skin for footwear and the presence of a riding whip among the same body of objects both point to a wardrobe built around mounted herding life: the half-nomadic Bashkirs travelled through the mountains or the steppes with their cattle, and recruitment into the Russian army and heavy taxation under the Russian Empire pressed many of them towards a settled life and away from that nomadic pastoralism. The sources used do not describe women's garments, belts, or a ceremonial dress distinct from everyday wear.

### Architecture

The sources used for this profile do not cover Bashkir house forms, building materials or architectural ornament.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The catalogued Bashkir objects are overwhelmingly of wood, bone, leather and horn rather than clay or metal. Archery equipment comes as a set: a bow of wood and horn, a leather bow case, a leather quiver and a group of arrows, alongside a knife with a bone blade and a leather sheath. Household and dairy equipment is turned and carved: wooden spoons, a wooden soup ladle, wooden basins made for *kumis*, and the *chelak*, a wooden honey barrel. Two specialised wooden forms stand out — the holiday scoop, fitted with a chain, of which several examples are held, and a bee-collecting ladle, the direct material trace of the wild-hive beekeeping practised in the Burzyansky District near the Kapova Cave. A riding whip completes the equestrian kit.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used describe no Bashkir jewelry as such; the only body adornment attested is the beadwork on the man's shirt, where white and green glass beads are grouped in threes along the applied red neckline trim, with one group of yellow beads.

## Music & performance

The central Bashkir instrument is the *quray*, an end-blown flute made from a reed found only in the Ural Mountains; it is the most important instrument in the Bashkir ensemble and is played in both traditional and modern popular music, among others by Zahir Bayiq. Song genres sit inside a broader oral repertoire that the sources describe as including ritual, epic and lyrical song alongside epic and fairy tales, legends, traditions and riddles. The documentation of this music began with the ethnographer S. G. Rybakov, whose *Music and Songs of the Ural's Muslims and Studies of Their Way of Life* appeared in 1897 as the first major study of music in Bashkortostan; L. N. Lebedinskiy collected numerous folk songs in the republic from 1930 onwards. Institutional support followed: the Ufa State Institute of Arts, founded in 1968 and later named for Zagir Ismagilov, sponsored research and teaches a dedicated Bashkir music faculty, and a network of conservatories and colleges — Ufa College of Arts (1921), the Bashkir Republican College of Culture and Art at Sterlitamak (1933), Salawat College of Music (1961), the music college at Oktyabrsky (1969), Uchaly College of Arts and Culture (1972) and Sibay College of the Arts (1997) — carries the training further. The National Symphonic Orchestra of the Bashkortostan Republic was founded in 1992 under Tahir Kamalov and became one of the major symphonies of late twentieth-century Russia. Music in Bashkortostan is shared with the Russians, Tatars, Chuvash, Mari, Udmurts and Ukrainians who live there.

## Dance & theatre

The sources record the professionalisation of Bashkir dance rather than a repertoire of named dances: G. Gaskarav, the first artistic leader of Bashkir folk theatrical choreography, founded a professional folk dance ensemble in 1939, and the company has since toured widely. Theatre is present institutionally, as a faculty of the Ufa State Institute (Academy) of Arts. The sources used name no individual dances, mask or puppet traditions, and do not distinguish ceremonial from entertainment forms.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not set out an annual Bashkir festival calendar, but they describe several occasions in detail. *Kaz-oemahe* is a work-and-feast gathering: the hostess invites her neighbours to help process geese, and at the end of the day's work treats everyone to fresh goose. Weddings carry the densest ritual food obligations. The bride prepares *chak-chak*, and after the ceremony, with washed hands, places a piece of it in the mouth of every guest — an obligatory part of the wedding rite. Small dumplings called *keyeu-bilmene* are made for the wedding in honour of the groom, and the bride also makes a special noodle, which must be especially thin and crumbly, as a demonstration of her skill. At festive meals it is customary to offer each guest *ulush*, their portion of the game — ram, goose and so on. Hospitality itself is codified: food is served as soon as a guest arrives, flatbread is set out in an odd number and never fewer than the number of guests, the host tastes first and the oldest guest is served first, the host stops eating when the guest stops, and if food is short the host eats as little as possible so the guest is satisfied. Food and drink are taken only with the right hand, fresh bread is not cut with a knife, one takes the poorer food from a shared dish and leaves the best for others, peace and good cheer are kept through the meal, and it closes with a prayer for the host's well-being.

## Foodways

Bashkir cooking rests on cattle breeding and on a semi-nomadic need for food that keeps: boiled, dried and jerked horse meat and lamb, dairy, dried berries, dried cereals and honey. Spicing is deliberately spare — only black and red pepper — and meat is abundant in every hot dish and snack. *Qazı* is a horse sausage, and horse meat is eaten in thick slices with fat, washed down with the sour fermented-milk *qurut* (also *qorot*, a young dry cheese) to cut the richness. Other keeping foods include *qaqlanğan et* (jerky), pastille, *siyəli harı may* (cherry in ghee), *moyıl mayı* (bird cherry oil), *irimsik* (cottage cheese) and *ayran*. The signature dish is *beshbarmaq* (*bishbarmaq*), boiled meat with *salma* or *halma*, coarsely chopped noodles, heaped with herbs and onions and seasoned with *qurut* or sour cream (*qaymaq*). *Boða* is a wheat or oatmeal drink; *üyrə* and *horpa* are soups; *qað*, *qatlama*, *mantı*, *ıvmas aşı* and *bukken* are shared with peoples from the Urals to the Far East. *Qımıð* (koumiss), fermented mare's milk, is the national healing drink, made from the milk of the Bashkir horse, drunk fresh before it sours, and said to have been made on the move in a vessel hung from the saddle. Bashkir honey, from the Burzyan bee, is a point of family honour and no tea party happens without it. Tea is always taken with milk — guests are not asked — and "drinking tea" means a spread of pies, boiled meat, sausage, cheesecake, sour cream, jam and honey substantial enough to replace a meal. Festive tables add *belish*, *gubadia* and obligatory chak-chak. Religious prohibitions bar pork, carnivorous animals and birds of prey such as falcon, kite and hoopoe, snake and frog; swans and cranes are Bashkir totems and not eaten; thyroid glands, spinal cord and spleen are avoided, as are fish without scales.

## Oral tradition & literature

Bashkir folklore is the strongest-documented intangible tradition here, preserving ancient views of nature, wisdom, psychology and moral ideals across epic and fairy tales, legends and traditions, riddles and song. The epics descend from ancient Turkic mythology and are described as a more developed and expanded form of that older epic culture; most were written down and published as books in the early twentieth century, where they form a large part of Bashkir literature. The central work is ***Ural Batyr***, which tells of the hero Ural and gives the Ural Mountains their name. Its world is three-tiered: the heavenly king Samrau lives in the sky with the Sun and the Moon as his wives and the daughters Umay and Aikhylu, who appear as birds or as beautiful girls — Umay first as a swan; people live on the earth, the best of them honouring nature; and beneath lies the underworld of the Devas, snake-formed powers of darkness. Ural destroys the deva and obtains the "living water", a dualistic framing of good and evil rooted in the pre-Islamic Bashkir conception of the world. Other epics central to Bashkir identity are ***Aqbuzat***, ***Qara yurga***, ***Aqhaq qola***, ***Kongur buga*** and ***Uzaq Tuzaq***. Genealogical tradition is recorded in *shezhere*, Bashkir family trees, which preserve material about the sixteenth century that is otherwise lost. A legend of origin explains the ethnonym itself: a wolf sent to guide the first seven Bashkir tribes from the Syr Darya valley to the land granted them by the Tengrist fertility goddess Umay, hence *bash* ("head, leader") and *qurt* (an archaic word for wolf) — "leading wolf".

## Language & religion

Bashkir is a Kipchak Turkic language, co-official with Russian in Bashkortostan, with roughly 1.6 million native speakers and three dialect groups: Southern, Eastern and North-Western. It is agglutinative and SOV, with heavy Russian, Arabic and Persian borrowing, and is set apart from its close relative Tatar by the dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ — as in *duś* "friend" or *hüź* "word", where Tatar has *süz* — by word-initial /s/ becoming /h/, and by explicitly written labial vowel harmony. A runic inscription of the ninth century is the first attestation of a Bashkir language. After the adoption of Islam from the tenth century the Bashkirs wrote in Turki, in an Arabic-based script; a purpose-built Arabic alphabet and a literary standard followed in 1923, the Unified Turkic Latin Alphabet in 1930, and an adapted Cyrillic in 1939. Most Bashkirs today are bilingual in Bashkir and Russian, and most are Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi madhhab following the Jadid doctrine; the older Tengrist layer, with its sky god, twelve powers of nature recorded by Ibn Fadlan in 922 and the goddess Umay, survives inside the epic repertoire.

Bashkir material culture centers on objects for herding life, archery, dairy work, and beekeeping, made chiefly from wood, bone, leather, horn and felt.

Bashkir textiles use cream and red linen or felt with simple leaf motifs and red cotton trim.

title: "Nanai"
subtitle: "Russia"
region: "East Asia"

## Overview

The Nanai (Russian *nanaitsy*, from *nanai* / *nani*, "natives, locals, people of the land") are a Tungusic people of the Middle Amur Basin, living along the Amur (Heilongjiang), Songhua (Sunggari) and Ussuri (Wusuli) rivers. In Russia they are settled downstream of Khabarovsk on both sides of Komsomolsk-on-Amur, on the Ussuri and Girin rivers and toward the Sea of Okhotsk; the 2010 census counted 12,003. In China they are one of the 56 officially recognised ethnic groups, known as *Hezhe*, numbering 4,640 in the 2000 census, mostly in Heilongjiang. Their language belongs to the Manchu-Tungusic family. Their descent is traced to the Wild Jurchens of northernmost Manchuria. In folk-culture terms the Nanai are known above all for garments cut and sewn from tanned fish skin — a practice that earned them the exonym "Fish-skin Tartars" (*Yúpí Dázi*) — and for Amur shamanic practice.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Fish-skin garment work** — Clothing was made from fish skins: the skins were dried, struck repeatedly with a mallet until completely smooth, and sewn together, with fish weighing more than 50 kilograms selected for the purpose. A woman's costume in the Museum of Ethnography (Stockholm), acquired in 1926 from the Russian Museum of Ethnography in St Petersburg, is made of burbot skins.

**Fish-skin appliqué** — Cut-and-stitched appliqué in white fish skin over dyed fish-skin ground, as on a pair of fish-skin leggings (or sleeves) in the British Museum: tapered, with a semi-circular top, dyed blue with a darker lower third turning yellow toward the hem, carrying large circular scroll appliqués and much smaller motifs below, lined with cream tabby linen.

**Cloth appliqué on leather and fur** — A British Museum quiver of leather and fur, made in six horizontally stitched sections, carries a square cloth appliqué below the opening and on the flap, its scrolls picked out in cream tabby linen against a blue (indigo-dyed) ground, outlined in green, yellow and blue yarns, with fur appliqué across the remaining front.

**Embroidered collars** — A man's collar in the British Museum has a dark blue tabby ground worked with scroll patterning in buttonhole stitch and isolated scrolls in chain stitch, its hem carrying threaded glass beads and suspended pendants.

**Pieced cloth and embroidery samples** — An incomplete British Museum domestic cloth doubling as an embroidery sample is built from small triangles of cream and dark blue tabby cotton patched into a ten-by-ten grid of squares.

Ornament was not purely decorative: on the Stockholm costume the garment edges symbolised the life force of the river, and the patterning carried a protective power derived from the maker's creative energy. A woman who could make strong patterns held high status. Many such garments show Chinese influence in their patterning.

**Motif vocabulary.** Scrolls (the dominant element, both continuous and isolated); circular appliqué medallions; curved two-tone motifs on footwear; diamond-set bead grids on collar hems; and, on shaman's gear, serpents, lizards and frogs, with branching horns on the hat.

### Clothing & dress

Everyday dress was fish skin, dried and mallet-softened, and fur. Surviving pieces indicate a layered wardrobe: a woman's full fish-skin costume; tapered fish-skin leggings or sleeves; a splayed arc-shaped collar for men, beaded and hung with stone and pearl-like pendants; and cloth boots whose lower leg and sole are cream tabby cotton, the sole quilted in self-colour thread, with a pale blue band at mid-boot and, above it, yellow cloth carrying dark blue and cream curved appliqué outlined in cream, pink and blue thread. Hair was politically marked: Amur peoples already wore a queue at the back of the head, and the Qing ordered the front of all male heads shaved after conquest, so that the Ulch called the Nanai "shaved-head people". Shaman's dress stood apart from daily wear — a skirt and jacket, a leather belt hung with conical metal pendants, mittens figured with serpents, lizards or frogs, and a hat with branching horns or with bear, wolf or fox fur attached; fragments of Chinese mirrors were sometimes worked into the costume.

### Architecture

The sources used here describe settlement rather than building: the people on the Ussuri lived in villages along the river banks, and three ethnic Nanai villages remain in Russia — Dzhuen, Ulika and Dada — but they say nothing about house form, materials, roofing or architectural ornament.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Household and hunting equipment in the collections is of bark, skin, wood and leather rather than clay. Birch bark was worked into lidded boxes (a box and its separate cover are catalogued at the British Museum). Fish skin served containers as well as clothing, in the form of a sewn pouch. A knife survives as a wooden handle. The long rectangular quiver described above, with its top flap, side ties and fastening ties, is of leather and fur. The only worked metal the sources name is the set of conical pendants on the shaman's leather belt, alongside pieces of Chinese mirror incorporated into shamanic costume. Nothing in the sources describes Nanai pottery.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment appears in the sources as part of garment construction rather than as separate ornament. The British Museum collar carries cream, light blue and dark blue glass beads of different sizes threaded in a diamond pattern along the hem, and below the beadwork a row of suspended pendants made of semi-precious stones and pearl-like beads. Shamanic regalia adds conical metal pendants hung from a leather belt and inset fragments of Chinese mirror. One funerary body marking is documented: in preparing the rite for a dead infant it was common to mark the body with coal, for instance by drawing a bracelet around the wrist, so that a later child born with similar markings could be recognised as the same soul returned. The sources do not cover tattooing or hairdressing beyond the Qing-imposed shaving of the forehead.

## Music & performance

Documented Nanai performance divides between shamanic ritual sound and twentieth-century professional music. Shamanic practice rests on the shaman's expulsion of bad spirits through prayers to the gods, and on the voice carrying the souls of the dead toward the underworld in the three-day *kasa tavori*. One such ritual voice was recorded commercially: the Nanai female shaman Tchotghtguerele Chalchin performed an incantation recorded in Siberia for the song "The Lighthouse" — an adaptation of Wilfrid Wilson Gibson's poem "Flannan Isle" — on the French producer Hector Zazou's 1994 album *Chansons des mers froides* (Songs from the Cold Seas), with lead vocals by Siouxsie Sioux and backing by the Sakharine Percussion Group and the Sissimut Dance Drummers. The best-known Nanai singer is Kola Beldy (1929–1993), popular across the Soviet Union and Russia and particularly identified with his rendition of "Увезу тебя я в тундру" ("I will take you to the tundra"). On the Chinese side, the Hezhen have a body of oral literature called *Yimakan*, which belongs as much to performance as to literature. The sources name no Nanai musical instruments and describe no wedding or seasonal song repertoire, so instrument names and song genres are left out here rather than supplied from elsewhere.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used for this profile name no Nanai dance or dramatic tradition; the only staged or choreographed material they mention is the dog-sledge procession of soul figures within the funerary ritual described below.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources document no annual festival calendar, but they describe the funerary cycle in unusual detail. The Nanai hold that each person has both a soul and a spirit, and that the body is only the soul's outer shell — a belief original to them rather than introduced by Christianity. At death the two part ways: the spirit turns malevolent and begins to harm living relatives, and these *amban* may in time be tamed and afterwards worshipped, or else driven off by a special ritual. The soul is first placed in a temporary cloth shelter called a *lachako*, where it stays seven days, then moved into a wooden doll, a *panyo*. The *panyo* is treated as a living person: the closest family member puts it to bed each night with a miniature pillow and blanket and wakes it in the morning, carries it along when travelling, and occasionally sets a pipe into the small hole carved for its mouth so the dead may smoke. The final rite, *kasa tavori*, lasts three days with much feasting; on the third day the souls pass from the *panyo* into large human-shaped wooden figures made to the height of the deceased, called *mugdeh*, which are loaded onto a dog sledge for the journey to the underworld, *Buni*. Before departure the shaman relays the dead's last wishes to the assembled family — in the anthropologist Gaer's account, one soul asked that a debt to a neighbour be repaid. The shaman then leads the sledges on the dangerous journey and must leave *Buni* before sunset or die. Afterwards relatives formerly neither visited the graves nor spoke of the dead. Children under a year are reckoned birds rather than people: an infant's soul flies off as a bird, the body is wrapped in birch-bark paper and placed high in a forest tree — a "wind burial" — and the soul is free to enter a woman again.

## Foodways

The river economy was the food economy. Early visitors, including the French Jesuit geographers who travelled the Ussuri and Amur in 1709, found a people whose subsistence was based on fishing: villagers spent whole summers at it, eating fish fresh in summer — sturgeon was especially prized — and drying the surplus for winter. Fish also fed the few domestic animals they kept, which made the flesh of a locally raised pig close to inedible for visitors with European tastes. Agriculture arrived slowly, and in 1709 practically the only crop grown by the villagers on the Ussuri shores was tobacco. Fire itself belonged to the food hearth as a person: it was personified as an elderly woman, *Fadzya Mama*, whom small children were not allowed to startle by running up to the fire and in whose presence men were always courteous. Beyond the three days of feasting at *kasa tavori*, the sources name no ceremonial dishes, drinks or dietary rules, and no vernacular dish names, so none are given.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Chinese Hezhen possess a rich oral literature known as *Yimakan*. Nanai cosmology carries its own narrative material: the land was once flat until great serpents gouged out the river valleys, and every thing in the universe holds a spirit that wanders the world independently. The Nanai share one myth with southern Chinese, and some Han Chinese are said to have founded clan subdivisions among them. The best-known Nanai figure in world literature is not an author but a subject — Dersu Uzala, the Nanai guide and friend of the Russian explorer Vladimir Arsenyev, who wrote about him in two books later adapted by Akira Kurosawa in his 1975 film *Dersu Uzala*. Written Nanai literature is a Soviet and post-Soviet project: folklore materials were published from the 1980s and 1990s, and Nanai-language books, including poetry and children's fairy tales, were issued at Khabarovsk by writers such as G. Bel'dy, E. Samar and A. Passar, alongside Valentin Avrorin's Nanai translation of a Russian children's play.

## Language & religion

Nanai (also called Gold, Goldi or Hezhen; *Hèzhéyǔ* in China) is Manchu-Tungusic, with about 1,400 speakers out of some 17,000 ethnic Nanai. Dialects fall into middle and lower Amur groups (Naykhin, Dzhuen, Bolon, Ekon, Gorin and others), plus Kur-Urmi near Khabarovsk, Bikin on the middle Ussuri and Sungari on the Chinese side; classifications by Sunik, Avrorin and Sem differ, and teaching based on the Naykhin dialect has levelled the distinctions. Writing passed through missionary Cyrillic in the late nineteenth century, a Unified Northern Alphabet Latin script approved in January 1932, and Cyrillic again from 1937, the current alphabet dating from 1993; in China Nanai write in Chinese, and a Hezhe schoolbook in pinyin transcription appeared in 2005. Russian teaching continues in 13 schools in Khabarovsk. The Nanai are mainly Shamanist, revering the bear (*Doonta*) and the tiger (*Amba*) and worshipping the spirits of sun, moon, mountains, water and trees; many are also Tibetan Buddhist.

## At a glance

| Who | Nanai people, a Tungusic ethnic group |
| Where | Middle Amur Basin along the Amur, Songhua and Ussuri rivers in Russia and China |

## Overview

The Nanai are a Tungusic people living along the Amur and Ussuri rivers in Russia and China, descended from the Wild Jurchens of northern Manchuria. They are renowned for clothing made from tanned fish skin, earning them the name "Fish-skin Tartars". Their culture centers on shamanic practice, an intricate funerary cycle involving wooden soul figures, and a river-based economy centered on fishing.

## Material culture

Nanai material culture is built from the river: fish skin for garments, birch bark for boxes, wood and leather for tools and ritual objects, with appliqué and embroidery as the main decorative arts.

### Textile & pattern traditions

The Nanai made clothing and decorated objects from fish skin, dried and softened by mallet-striking, with cut-and-stitched appliqué and embroidery in scrolls and geometric patterns.

- **Fish-skin garment work** — Skins were dried, struck repeatedly with a mallet until smooth, then sewn together, with fish weighing more than 50 kilograms selected for the purpose.
- **Fish-skin appliqué** — White fish skin was cut and stitched onto dyed fish-skin ground in large circular scroll and smaller motifs, as on leggings with blue dye and darker lower thirds.
- **Cloth appliqué on leather and fur** — Square cloth appliqués with scroll patterning in cream linen against indigo ground were stitched onto leather and fur quivers, outlined in green, yellow and blue yarns.
- **Embroidered collars** — Dark blue cloth collars carried scroll patterning in buttonhole and chain stitch, with threaded glass beads and suspended pendants along the hem.

### Clothing & dress

Everyday dress was fish skin and fur, layered and tapered, with decorated collars, leggings and cloth boots; shamanic dress was separate and more elaborate.

- **Woman's full fish-skin costume** — A complete outfit made from fish skin, with examples recorded from the early 20th century showing the full range of garment construction and appliqué decoration.
- **Splayed arc-shaped collar** — A decorative men's collar with beading and suspended stone and pearl-like pendants, marking status and formal wear.
- **Cloth boots** — Boots with cream tabby cotton lower leg and sole, quilted in self-colour thread, with pale blue band at mid-boot and yellow cloth carrying dark blue and cream curved appliqué.
- **Shaman's costume** — A skirt and jacket with leather belt hung with conical metal pendants, mittens figured with serpents and lizards, and a hat with branching horns or fur.

### Architecture

The Nanai lived in villages along river banks, with three ethnic villages remaining in Russia, but sources provide no details about house form or construction.

- **Nanai villages** — Three ethnic Nanai villages remain in Russia: Dzhuen, Ulika and Dada, settled on river banks.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Household and hunting equipment was made from natural materials—bark, skin, wood and leather—rather than clay or cast metal.

- **Birch-bark boxes** — Lidded containers made from birch bark, with separate covers, used for storage.
- **Fish-skin pouches** — Sewn containers made from fish skin, serving both practical and symbolic functions.
- **Leather and fur quiver** — Long rectangular hunting quiver with top flap and side ties, made in six horizontally stitched sections, decorated with cloth and fur appliqué.
- **Conical metal pendants** — Worked metal ornaments hung from shamanic leather belts, among the few metal objects documented in collections.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment appeared primarily as part of garment construction rather than separate ornament, using glass beads, semi-precious stones and shamanic metal pieces.

- **Beaded collar hems** — Cream, light blue and dark blue glass beads threaded in diamond patterns along garment hems, often with suspended pendants of semi-precious stones and pearl-like beads.
- **Coal body marks for funerary rites** — Coal markings drawn on an infant's body during funerary preparation, such as bracelets around the wrist, to identify the soul if it returned in a later child.
- **Shamanic mirror insets** — Fragments of Chinese mirrors worked into shamanic costume as spiritual protection.

## Music & performance

Nanai performance included shamanic ritual voice for expelling spirits and guiding souls, and 20th-century professional singers.

- **Kasa tavori incantations** (*kasa tavori*) — Shamanic ritual voices recorded during the three-day funerary rite, with the shaman's voice carrying souls of the dead toward the underworld.
- **Kola Beldy** — The best-known Nanai singer (1929–1993), popular across the Soviet Union and identified with his rendition of "I will take you to the tundra".
- **Yimakan oral literature** (*Yimakan*) — A body of oral literature of the Chinese Hezhen people, belonging as much to performance as to written tradition.

## Dance & theatre

No Nanai dance or dramatic tradition is documented in sources; the only staged material mentioned is the dog-sledge procession of soul figures in funerary ritual.

## Festivals & rituals

The Nanai funerary cycle is elaborate and detailed: the soul and spirit part at death, the soul moves through temporary cloth shelter, wooden doll, and finally large wooden figures for the journey to the underworld.

- **Lachako** — A temporary cloth shelter where the soul rests for seven days after death before moving into a wooden figure.
- **Panyo** — A wooden doll into which the soul is placed after leaving the lachako, treated as a living person with pillow, blanket and miniature pipe.
- **Mugdeh** — Large human-shaped wooden figures made to the height of the deceased, loaded onto a dog sledge for the journey to the underworld Buni.
- **Kasa tavori** — The three-day final funerary rite with much feasting, in which souls pass from the panyo into mugdeh figures for the underworld journey.
- **Wind burial** — Infants under one year are placed in birch-bark paper wrapping high in a forest tree, their souls freed to enter another woman as a bird.

## Foodways

The Nanai subsistence was based on river fishing, with sturgeon especially prized, supplemented by dried fish for winter and small amounts of tobacco agriculture.

- **Sturgeon** — The most prized fish species in the Nanai diet, eaten fresh in summer and dried for winter.
- **Fadzya Mama** — The fire personified as an elderly woman, respected as a person—children were not allowed to startle her and men were always courteous in her presence.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Nanai possess cosmological narratives, and written literature is a Soviet and post-Soviet project, while the Chinese Hezhen maintain a rich oral tradition called Yimakan.

- **Nanai cosmology** — The Nanai creation narrative holds that great serpents gouged out the river valleys in a once-flat land, and every thing in the universe holds an independent spirit.
- **Dersu Uzala** — A Nanai guide and friend of Russian explorer Vladimir Arsenyev, the subject of two books later adapted by Akira Kurosawa in his 1975 film.
- **Yimakan** — The rich oral literature of the Chinese Hezhen people, with narrative and performance traditions.

## Language & religion

Nanai is Manchu-Tungusic with about 1,400 speakers; the Nanai are mainly Shamanist, revering the bear and tiger and worshipping spirits of nature.

- **Nanai language** (*Nanai*) — Also called Gold, Goldi or Hezhen; Manchu-Tungusic with dialects including Naykhin, Dzhuen, Bolon and others, taught in 13 schools in Khabarovsk.
- **Doonta** — The bear, a revered animal spirit in Nanai Shamanism.
- **Amba** — The tiger, a revered animal spirit in Nanai Shamanism.
- **Buni** — The underworld to which souls travel in the mugdeh wooden figures, reached via dog sledge.

## Overview

The Mongols are an East Asian people native to Mongolia and to China — Inner Mongolia and eleven other autonomous territories — as well as to parts of southern Siberia; the contiguous area they chiefly inhabit is called the Mongol heartland. They are the principal member of the wider family of Mongolic peoples, and their indigenous dialects are grouped together as the Mongolian language. The Oirats and the Buryats are classified either as separate ethno-linguistic groups or as Mongol subgroups. A common descent from the Proto-Mongols binds them, and their history as a single political body runs from the Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan through the Northern Yuan to the Qing submission of 1691. In folk-culture terms they matter as mobile pastoralists: nearly 80 per cent of Mongolian territory is pasture, and livestock — more than twenty million head of wool-bearing sheep, cattle, camels, goats and horses — remains the country's most important economic activity.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The catalogue records behind this gallery document three pattern-bearing textile objects rather than a set of named weaving schools, so the entries below are object-level traditions.

**Khalkha woman's silk costume** — A complete set of dress for a wealthy Khalkha woman, built around a blue silk suit and worn with a braided cloth headpiece, a silver crown, pearl-band ornaments, earrings and a chest ornament. The Museum of Ethnography set was stolen and recovered twenty-five years later.

**Torghut silk damask robe** — A mid-green robe of silk damask from Etsin gol, its woven ground patterned with flowers and ornaments and overlaid with applied bands in black and gold-metal thread worked in a complex pattern weave; the applied motif may be lotus flowers. Cords, braid and machine-woven bands edge the standing collar, the fastening and the waist, and two embroidered breast pockets of green and purple plain-weave cloth are set into the front.

**Piled-wool prayer rug** — A square prayer carpet woven of piled red wool and backed with off-white cotton.

**Motif vocabulary.** Dragons (on knife handles, sheath mounts and an amulet case); twin fishes at the end of a knife handle; the eternity knot, worked in silver on a wooden bowl; the eight Buddhist emblems, likewise in silver on a bowl; whirling emblems on a knife sheath; a bird on both faces of a silver snuff bottle; a bat framing the glass front of an amulet case; flowers and ornaments woven into silk damask; fish, as the whole form of a silver pipe cleaner.

### Clothing & dress

Men's and women's dress in this collection diverge sharply in ornament. The wealthy Khalkha woman's outfit described above is a layered assembly of blue silk, silver and pearl, crowned with a silver headdress and finished with earrings and a hanging chest ornament; a Torghut woman's robe of green silk damask carries its decoration in applied bands and braid rather than in embroidery alone. Photographs taken at Chailar (Chulun) show women in a long dress worn with a short coat and a cap, standing before wooden houses. Men's dress in the same photographs is working dress: a herder posed with a steppe horse, horse-dealers seated on the sill of a wooden house holding a saddled animal by the rein. One man's hat survives in detail — conical, built up from coiled and plaited bast, with long red-dyed yak hair glued to the sides, a domed silver base at the top (its finial now missing), a lining of red tabby cotton and a padded headband and straps of the same cloth. Belt furniture was its own category of dress: a knife in its sheath, a fire-steel and a pair of bone chopsticks were carried together on a hanger. Ceremonial dress at the far end of the range is a Mongolian warrior's armour in thirteen parts — helmet, jacket, chest guard and back guard among them — still worn as parade costume by the bodyguards of certain chieftains when it was collected.

### Architecture

The characteristic dwelling is the *ger*, the demountable house of Mongolia's nomads, built from the raw materials to hand and framed in carved and polychrome-painted wood. Its logic is movement: a pastoral life that covers long distances in search of new grazing requires a house that can be struck and reassembled, and the *ger* answers that. Photographs from the Mongolian steppe show a man standing in front of one beside a section of plaited wicker enclosure — the pen and the tent together forming the working unit of the camp — and other camp views show two-wheeled carts drawn up among the tents. At Chailar (Chulun) the same photographic series records fixed wooden houses, with people posed at their doors and window sills, so settled timber building and portable felt-and-wood building existed side by side in the places the collectors passed through. Religious architecture appears only indirectly, through its furniture and through the temples where objects were bought: the lama temple Tung Scheng Chao, visited on 30 April 1930, and the monastery of Khadain-sume, also written Hattin sume, where much of the Swedish collection was acquired.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Metal dominates. Vessels include a copper teapot with movable handles and a sunken lid, blackened by use and identified as Chinese in type; a brass vessel with hanging-mount handles and a copper loop for a knob, used to ladle food from the cauldron at feasts and carry it into the tent; and a two-handled bronze temple jug with visible casting seams. Wooden bowls were lined and mounted in silver, one with the eternity knot, another with a silver foot and the eight Buddhist emblems — its wood especially valued because it came from Tibet. Lighter household gear includes a birch-bark box with a wooden base and handled lid, recorded as a milk container, and a back-carrier called *urch* or *urck*: two double wooden bows with crossbars, joined below by leather straps and slung from braces of sewn cattle-hair rope. Folding altar tables, *Taxile'en sjirae*, were made in pairs by Sagetjin Baell Mongols, assembled without nails or screws and painted red with gilded ornament on the visible faces.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Silver set with coral is the signature. The collection holds silver rings each set with a single coral; silver bracelets, one slightly triangular in section, decorated with a Chinese good-fortune character; and a pair of silver hair ornaments for a woman, coral-studded, brass-backed with a hook and joined by a thread, 14.5 cm each and 49 cm overall. Two silver-and-coral side pendants were hung at a woman's sides and used to carry small objects: inside the outer ring runs a band of movable coral beads, and at the centre sits a movable openwork filigree ball of silver. Amulet cases were worn as well as kept — one round, of copper, pierced in openwork, from Sunit; another of white metal with a glass front framed by a bat and dragon-and-serpent ornament, an engraved sign on the back, and inside it a pale cloth holding powder. Of hair practice the Wikipedia source records only the thirteenth-century style in which men shaved the head but for three locks, the side strands plaited to hang at the shoulders.

## Music & performance

One instrument is documented in detail, and it is enough to be specific about. The *hore*, described in the collection notes as a kind of violin, is a two-stringed bowed chordophone with a wooden resonator whose sides are dovetailed together; the underside is closed with riveted sheet brass and the upper face covered with leather, pierced at the centre by a coin-shaped sound hole. The sides are painted gold and decorated with trailing scrollwork, the neck carries three bands of bone, and the instrument has two tuning pegs. Its bow is wood and horsehair, the wooden stick painted red. The instrument reached Sweden in 1929 in a consignment of religious objects from Mongolia and Tibet, which places it in the same acquisition context as altar tables and amulet cases rather than in a described performance setting. Beyond this, the sources used here give no account of song genres, singers or occasions for music, with one exception noted below: a bead chain worn by priests at the New Year festival of the god of heaven, which implies liturgical performance without describing it.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used here say nothing about Mongol dance or theatrical traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

Two ritual occasions surface in the catalogue records. The first is a New Year festival addressed to the god of heaven, at which priests wore a chain of 108 wooden beads strung with four large pale-red glass beads and finished with wound thread and brass fittings, wrapped around the neck; an attached label identifies the piece as an official's chain of the Qing period, so the same object type served both office and liturgy. The second is the feast, for which a brass vessel with hanging handles was used to empty cooked food from the cauldron and carry it into the tent where the guests were served — an ordinary vessel whose recorded use is entirely festive. Monastic ritual is present in the objects without a described calendar: paired folding altar tables with gilded fronts, amulet cases containing powder wrapped in cloth, and three undecorated skull bowls forming a linked set. Collecting itself was timed to the ritual year — the 1930 trip into Mongolia set out three days before New Year's Eve, with a Mongolian lama named Chagdur travelling with the party, and the amulet cases and hair ornaments were bought at Khadain-sume on 3 and 5 January. The sources do not cover birth, coming-of-age, wedding or funeral rites.

## Foodways

Foodways here are the foodways of herders. Pastoralism is the basis of the traditional economy, and the herds named in the collection record — sheep, cattle, camels, goats and horses, more than twenty million head in Mongolia — define what the kitchen handled: meat and milk. Milk was stored and carried in a birch-bark box with a wooden base and a handled wooden lid. Cooking was done in a cauldron, and at feasts the food was lifted out into a handled brass vessel and carried into the tent to be served. Eating equipment travelled on the body: a knife with an iron blade and a wooden handle riveted in brass or iron and faced with white metal, carried in a wooden sheath with silver or white-metal mounts, with a pair of bone chopsticks pushed into two holes in the sheath and, on the fuller set, a fire-steel on the same belt hanger. Drinking vessels were wooden bowls lined inside with raised silver, one a tea bowl whose Tibetan wood was prized in itself. Tea was boiled or served in a copper pot with movable handles, blackened by long use. Alongside food, two habits of consumption are documented: snuff, taken from a round footed silver bottle called *Kuchur*, its lid originally set with five corals and fitted with a small spoon to dip into the flask; and smoking, attested by a fish-shaped pipe cleaner of silver said to have belonged to a chieftain near Khalun usu. The sources name no dishes.

## Oral tradition & literature

The written tradition is better documented in these sources than the oral one. Mongol-language historical writing includes the Secret History of the Mongols, cited as a thirteenth-century contemporary source, and two later chronicles, the *Erdeni-yin tobči* and the *Erdeni tunumal neretü sudur*; the latter records the embassy in which Altan Khan's envoys reminded the rulers of Moghulistan of their shared descent from Genghis Khan, and the former preserves a Chinggisid prince's remark, fleeing the Oirat ruler Esen Taishi, that "the khans of Toγmaγ, the descendants of Jochi, are our kindred." Mongol affairs were also written up from outside, in the Persian *Jami' al-tawarikh* and in the *Zafarnama* of Yazdi, where the Mongols of fifteenth-century Mongolia are called Qalmaqs. The ethnonym itself carries a folk etymology, derived in one proposal from a phrase meaning "eternal sky fire." The sources used here do not cover folktales, epic song, proverbs or riddles, nor present-day preservation work.

## Language & religion

Mongol dialects are collectively the Mongolian language, the central branch of the Mongolic family, whose earlier stages are traced through the Donghu confederation and the Xianbei; Middle Mongol sources of the late fourteenth century contain the first written references to the plough. Writing in the region predates Mongol script as recorded here: the Khitan, a Mongolic people, had two scripts of their own, and many Mongolic words are legible in their half-deciphered writings. Religion is layered. The culture of the post-Xianbei nomadic kingdoms is described as shamanist or Buddhist; by the seventeenth century Tibetan Buddhist factional politics ran through Mongol rule, with the Gelugpa, or Yellow Hat, sect backing the Manchus and the last khagan Ligdan supporting the Kagyu, or Red Hat, sect. Lamas, lama temples, altar tables, amulet cases and the eight Buddhist emblems on silverwork all belong to that establishment. Among the Kalmyks on the Volga, the Russian Orthodox church pressed Buddhists to convert.

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | Mongols, an East Asian people |
| Where | Mongolia, Inner Mongolia and parts of southern Siberia |
| How many | more than twenty million head of livestock |
| Language | Mongolian language |
| Religion | Tibetan Buddhism, shamanism |
| Known for | mobile pastoralists · nomadic ger dwellings · silver and coral jewelry · livestock herding · warrior traditions |

## Overview

The Mongols are an East Asian people native to Mongolia and parts of China and southern Siberia. Nearly eighty per cent of Mongolian territory is pasture, and livestock remains the country's most important economic activity. Their history as a single political body runs from the Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan through the Northern Yuan to the Qing submission of 1691. They matter as mobile pastoralists whose material culture reflects a life of movement and trade.

## Material culture

Metal and silver dominate Mongol material culture, paired with wood, felt, and coral in objects designed for portability and pastoral life.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Mongol textiles feature symbolic woven and applied patterns including dragons, fish, Buddhist emblems and ornaments.

- **Khalkha woman's silk costume** — A complete set of blue silk dress worn with braided cloth headpiece, silver crown, pearl-band ornaments, earrings and chest ornament.
- **Torghut silk damask robe** — A mid-green robe patterned with flowers and overlaid with applied bands in black and gold-metal thread, with embroidered breast pockets.
- **Piled-wool prayer rug** — A square prayer carpet woven of piled red wool and backed with off-white cotton.

### Clothing & dress

Men's and women's dress diverge sharply in ornament, from layered silk and silver for wealthy women to practical working dress for herders.

- **Man's conical hat** — Built up from coiled and plaited bast, with long red-dyed yak hair glued to the sides, a domed silver base at the top, and a red cotton lining.
- **Belt furniture** — A knife in its sheath, a fire-steel and a pair of bone chopsticks carried together on a hanger.
- **Mongolian warrior's armour** — Thirteen parts including helmet, jacket, chest guard and back guard, still worn as parade costume by bodyguards of certain chieftains.

### Architecture

The ger, a demountable house framed in carved and polychrome-painted wood, serves the logic of nomadic pastoral life.

- **Ger** — The demountable house of Mongolia's nomads, built from raw materials to hand and struck and reassembled as herds move to new grazing.
- **Plaited wicker enclosure** — A pen for animals forming a working unit of the camp together with the tent.
- **Tung Scheng Chao** — A lama temple visited on 30 April 1930 where religious objects were acquired.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Metal vessels dominate, with copper, brass and bronze pieces designed for cooking, serving and ceremonial use.

- **Copper teapot** — A Chinese-type vessel with movable handles and a sunken lid, blackened by use.
- **Brass vessel with hanging handles** — Used to ladle food from the cauldron at feasts and carry it into the tent.
- **Back-carrier** (*urch*) — Two double wooden bows with crossbars, joined by leather straps and slung from braces of sewn cattle-hair rope.
- **Folding altar table** (*Taxile'en sjirae*) — Made in pairs by Sagetjin Baell Mongols, assembled without nails or screws and painted red with gilded ornament on the visible faces.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Silver set with coral is the signature of Mongol jewelry, worn as rings, bracelets, hair ornaments and side pendants.

- **Silver rings with coral** — Each set with a single coral stone.
- **Silver bracelets** — Slightly triangular in section, decorated with a Chinese good-fortune character.
- **Silver hair ornaments** — Coral-studded, brass-backed with a hook and joined by thread, 14.5 cm each and 49 cm overall.
- **Silver-and-coral side pendants** — Hung at a woman's sides to carry small objects, with movable coral beads and a movable openwork filigree ball of silver at the centre.
- **Amulet case** — Round or with glass front framed by a bat and dragon ornament, containing powder wrapped in pale cloth.

## Music & performance

The hore, a two-stringed bowed chordophone, is the documented instrument, placed in the context of monastic rather than secular performance.

- **Hore** — A kind of violin with a wooden resonator whose sides are dovetailed together, closed with riveted sheet brass, upper face covered with leather and pierced with a coin-shaped sound hole.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used here say nothing about Mongol dance or theatrical traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

New Year festival and feasting mark the ritual calendar, with monastic altar tables, amulet cases and skull bowls serving religious practice.

- **New Year festival** — A festival addressed to the god of heaven at which priests wore a chain of 108 wooden beads strung with four large pale-red glass beads.
- **Official's chain** — A chain of 108 wooden beads with four large pale-red glass beads, wound thread and brass fittings, serving both Qing office and religious liturgy.
- **Feast** — A ceremonial occasion for which brass vessels with hanging handles were used to carry cooked food from the cauldron into the tent.

## Foodways

Foodways reflect pastoral herding, built on meat and milk from sheep, cattle, camels, goats and horses.

- **Birch-bark box** — A milk container with a wooden base and handled wooden lid.
- **Cauldron** — The cooking vessel from which food was lifted out for feasts.
- **Knife** — An eating tool with an iron blade and wooden handle riveted in brass or iron, faced with white metal, carried in a wooden sheath with silver or white-metal mounts.
- **Copper pot** — A tea vessel with movable handles, blackened by long use.
- **Snuff bottle** (*Kuchur*) — A round footed silver bottle whose lid was originally set with five corals and fitted with a small spoon.

## Oral tradition & literature

Written historical sources in Mongolian and Persian document Mongol affairs from the thirteenth century onward, while oral traditions remain undocumented here.

- **Secret History of the Mongols** — A thirteenth-century contemporary historical source written in Mongol.
- **Erdeni-yin tobči** — A later Mongol chronicle preserving a Chinggisid prince's remark about the khans of Toγmaγ as kindred.
- **Erdeni tunumal neretü sudur** — A Mongol chronicle recording an embassy in which Altan Khan's envoys reminded the rulers of Moghulistan of their shared descent from Genghis Khan.
- **Jami' al-tawarikh** — A Persian source documenting Mongol affairs from outside.
- **Zafarnama** — A work by Yazdi where the Mongols of fifteenth-century Mongolia are called Qalmaqs.

## Language & religion

Mongolian language belongs to the Mongolic family traced through Donghu and Xianbei, while religion blends shamanism and Tibetan Buddhism.

- **Mongolian language** — The central branch of the Mongolic family, with Mongol dialects collectively forming the group.
- **Mongol script** — A writing system developed by the Mongols, with earlier regional scripts like Khitan predating it.
- **Gelugpa** (*Yellow Hat*) — A Tibetan Buddhist sect backing the Manchus in seventeenth-century Mongol rule.
- **Kagyu** (*Red Hat*) — A Tibetan Buddhist sect supported by the last khagan Ligdan in seventeenth-century Mongol rule.

## Glossary

- *ger* — demountable house of nomads
- *urch* — back-carrier with wooden bows and leather straps
- *Taxile'en sjirae* — folding altar table
- *hore* — two-stringed bowed chordophone
- *Kuchur* — snuff bottle
- *Khalkha* — Mongol ethnic group
- *Torghut* — Mongol ethnic group
- *Qalmaqs* — term for Mongols of fifteenth-century Mongolia
- *Yellow Hat* — Gelugpa Buddhist sect
- *Red Hat* — Kagyu Buddhist sect
- *Genghis Khan* — founder of Mongol Empire
- *Altan Khan* — Mongol ruler who sent diplomatic envoys
- *Ligdan* — last khagan of the Mongols
- *lama* — Buddhist priest
- *Northern Yuan* — historical period in Mongol political history

## Overview

The Yi, who call themselves *Nuosu* (ꆈꌠ) and are known in Chinese as Yízú (彝族), are an ethnic group of southern China and the sixth largest of the 55 ethnic minorities recognized by the Chinese government; the 2020 census recorded 9,830,327 Yi. Over 4.5 million live in Yunnan, 2.5 million in southern Sichuan and 1 million in the northwest corner of Guizhou, with further populations in Guangxi; the Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture alone holds about two million. Across the border in northern Vietnam, 4,827 Lô Lô — a Yi subgroup — were counted in 2019 in Hà Giang, Cao Bằng and Lào Cai. Nearly all Yi live in mountainous country, often on steep slopes far from cities, and the sharp altitudinal differences between Yi districts produce the local saying that "the weather is different a few miles away." They speak Loloish (Yi) languages of the Tibeto-Burman family, closely related to Burmese, and possess their own script, used for centuries by *bimo* priests.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used here name no Yi weaving, embroidery, felting or dyeing tradition by its vernacular name, so no pattern tradition can be described. What they do document are the finished textile objects held in the museums this atlas draws on, all collected among the Yi at the Stone Forest in Yunnan in 1949 by Acher Eskenasy and L. van Bussel:

**Shoulder bag** — recorded in the Dutch catalogue as a travel bag (*reistas*) and in the collectors' own note simply as a "sholder bag"; several examples entered the collection together from the same Stone Forest acquisition.

**Baby carrier** — a cloth baby sling from the same 1949 Stone Forest group, catalogued as a baby carrier.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe Yi everyday or ceremonial dress, garment types, headgear, belts or footwear. Two points bearing on dress and appearance do appear in them: black is a revered colour in Yi culture, and the autonym Ni — the element behind Nuosu, Nasu, Nesu and Nisu — is sometimes translated as black for that reason. The museum objects shown alongside this profile are carried and worn accessories rather than garments: cotton shoulder bags and a baby carrier from the Stone Forest in Yunnan.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Yi house form, building materials, roof construction or architectural ornament. They record only the settlement pattern and one monumental practice: Yi villages lie on mountain slopes, the aristocratic and commoner castes historically lived in separate villages, and Old Yi stone tablets and steles stand in the Yi area, carrying texts in the pre-standardized script.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources name no Yi ceramic or metalworking tradition. One ritual object is catalogued in detail: a **family tablet** in the British Museum, classed at once as tablet, sculpture and religious or ritual equipment, and made of straw, wood, cotton cloth, bamboo and paper — a composite of perishable household materials rather than of carved stone or cast metal. The remaining documented everyday objects are the Stone Forest shoulder bags and baby carrier acquired in 1949. Two further material traditions are attested in the sources without being described as objects: the written transmission of Yi medical knowledge, which exists in records as well as in oral form, and the Old Yi stone tablets and steles.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not cover Yi jewelry, silverwork, tattooing or hair practice.

## Music & performance

The Yi play a range of instruments documented across their territory. Wind instruments include the *bawu* (巴乌) and the *mabu* (马布). They also play the *hulu sheng*, but — unlike other minority peoples of Yunnan — not for courtship or love songs (*aiqing*); the gourd pipe sits outside the Yi courtship repertoire. Large plucked and bowed string instruments are played as well. Among the Liangshan Yi the most commonly encountered instrument is the *kouxian*, a small four-pronged instrument comparable to a Jew's harp. Kouxian pieces are usually improvised rather than fixed, and are expected to reflect either the mood of the player or the surrounding environment; occasionally they too serve the *aiqing* function that the hulu sheng does not. Against this instrumental repertoire stands a body of ritual sound that the sources treat as religious rather than musical: the ritual texts transmitted in the Yi script by *bimo* priests from one generation to the next, and the exorcisms conducted against the ghost Jiegujienuo. The most publicly visible Yi performance form is dance, which the sources describe as the most commonly recognized kind of Yi musical performance.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name no individual Yi dance and no Yi dramatic or puppet tradition. They establish the performance context: Yi dance is the most widely recognized form of Yi musical performance and is frequently performed at publicly sponsored holidays and festival events — which, in the sources' account of the Yi calendar, means above all the Torch Festival.

## Festivals & rituals

The **Torch Festival** is one of the Yi people's main holidays and falls on the 24th day of the sixth month of the lunar calendar. Its legend tells of two men of great strength, Sireabi in heaven and Atilaba on earth. Hearing of Atilaba's strength, Sireabi challenged him to wrestle; after two defeats he was killed in a bout, and the enraged bodhisattvas sent a plague of locusts against the earth. Atilaba cut down pine trees and used them as torches to burn the locusts and save the crops, and the festival is held in his honour.

Life-cycle practice in the sources is dominated by descent, caste and death. Descent and inheritance were patrilineal, men practised polygamy and levirate marriage, and women were excluded from the oral genealogies. Caste membership in all four strata — the aristocratic *nuohuo*/nzymo Black Yi, the commoner *qunuo*/*quho* White Yi, the *ajia* and the *xiaxi* — passed by patrilineal descent, and the two upper castes did not intermarry; as late as the 1980s and early 1990s nuohuo clans still blocked or punished marriage with quho, and the ethnographer quoted in the sources notes that families feared being boycotted by other nuohuo if they married out. Funerary custom was a flashpoint with the state: under the Qing policy of *gaitu guiliu* and assimilation pressed by the Viceroy Ortai, Yi living near Kunming were forced to give up cremation for burial, which triggered rebellions that the dynasty suppressed. Ritual against misfortune is also recorded: the ghost Jiegujienuo, blamed for dizziness, slowness, dementia and anxiety, was fought with exorcisms for which the bimo erected sacred sticks, the *kiemobbur*, at the ritual site.

## Foodways

The sources used do not cover Yi staples, dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial food or drink traditions. They note only that Yi women drank and smoked noticeably more than Han Chinese women, and that farming was done by the White Yi and by slaves rather than by the Black Yi aristocracy.

## Oral tradition & literature

Yi oral tradition opens with an origin myth in which all life came from water, water came from snowmelt, and the dripping snowmelt formed a creature called the Ni, which gave birth to all life — Ni being another name for the Yi themselves. The common ancestor was *Apu Dumu* (ꀉꁌꅋꃅ / ꀉꁌꐧꃅ, Axpu Ddutmu or Axpu Jjutmu), whose three wives each bore two sons; the six sons migrated to the area of present-day Zhaotong and founded the Wu, Zha, Nuo, Heng, Bu and Mo clans. The great hero of Yi mythology is *Zhyge Alu*, son of a dragon and an eagle, possessed of supernatural strength and of powers against magic and ghosts, who rode a nine-winged flying horse called "long heavenly wings." He was helped by a magical peacock, *Shuotnyie Voplie*, whose cry deafened those who heard it but which consumed evil and expelled leprosy when invited indoors, and by the python *Bbahxa Ayuosse*, which he defeated by transforming into a dragon and wrestling it in the ocean, and which could detect leprosy, cure tuberculosis and eradicate epidemics. Like the Chinese archer Hou Yi, Zhyge Alu shoots down the suns to save the people; in Bimoism he aids the bimo in curing leprosy and fighting ghosts. Genealogical recitation is its own verbal art, chained father to son (Aho Ddezze—Ddezze Zuluo—Zuluo Jjiha—Jjiha Lomusse—Lomu Shuogge). Works of history, literature and medicine and ruling-family genealogies written in the Old Yi script remain in use. In contemporary documentation, the artist Colette Fu, great-granddaughter of the Yi military governor of Yunnan Long Yun, has photographed Yi communities in Yunnan from 1996 onward for her pop-up book series *We are Tiger Dragon People*.

## Language & religion

The Yi speak Loloish (also Ngwi or Nisoic) languages, a sub-branch of 50–100 Tibeto-Burman languages centred on Yunnan and most closely related to Burmese. The Chinese government recognizes six mutually unintelligible Yi languages: Northern Yi (Nuosu), Western Yi (Lalo), Central Yi (Lolopo), Southern Yi (Nisu), Southeastern Yi (Sani) and Eastern Yi (Nasu). Northern Yi, with some two million speakers, is the literary standard; code-switching with Standard Chinese is common in Yunnan, Guizhou and Guangxi. The Yi script, logosyllabic in origin and dating to at least the 13th century, appears independent of any other known script; it had perhaps 10,000 largely regional characters, was the preserve of bimo priests until the early 20th century, and was standardized into a syllabary in the 1970s and 1980s, now used in books, newspapers, street signs and schooling. The indigenous religion is **Bimoism**, served by the bimo. Some Yi in Yunnan have adopted Buddhism through contact with the Dai and Tibetans, their chief deity being Mahākāla; many converted to Christianity in the 20th century after Gladstone Porteous arrived in 1904 and China Inland Mission medical missionaries followed, and in 1991 as many as 1,500,000 Yi Christians were reported in Yunnan, concentrated in Luquan County with its more than 20 churches.

## Overview

The Dai are several Tai-speaking peoples of southern Yunnan, concentrated in the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture and the Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture, and counted by the People's Republic of China as one of its 56 officially recognized ethnic groups. "Dai" is a Han Chinese umbrella term with no equivalent in the Tai languages themselves, which have only broader words for Tai people in general; the groups it covers — speakers of *Tai Lü* (Sipsongpanna Dai) and *Tai Nüa* (Dehong Dai), of *Tai Dam* and of *Tai Ya* — are distinct culturally and linguistically. Figures compiled for Yunnan give roughly 400,000 speakers each for Tai Lü and Tai Nüa, about 40,000 for Tai Rui and about 20,000 for the Tianxin variety. In folk-culture terms the Dai matter as one of the few peoples native to China who practise Theravada Buddhism, with their own script, calendar and monastic literacy, and as cotton-and-silk weavers whose patterned cloth reached European museums in the twentieth century.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources document the Dai mainly through woven and embroidered cloth. Wikipedia names weaving first among Dai handicrafts, alongside oil-pressing, winemaking and bamboo work; the museum records give the fabrics themselves, without vernacular names for the techniques.

**Supplementary-weft cloth** — A fabric collected in 1949 at the Jinghong market in Xishuangbanna by Acher Eskenasy and L. van Bussel, and catalogued by the National Museum of World Cultures Foundation simply as untreated cloth woven with supplementary wefts: the pattern is carried by extra weft floats rather than printed or applied.

**Indigo patterned lengths** — Lengths of indigo cotton cloth with multi-coloured patterning and fringes worked at both ends, held by the British Museum.

**Patterned bedding cloth** — Cotton bedsheets and bed blankets in patterned weave, some fringed at one end only, together with a long narrow patterned mattress-cover; the same weaving repertoire serves the household as well as dress.

**Embroidered cloth** — A worked textile of cotton ground and cotton thread, and a two-part belt combining cotton and silk, both embroidered.

**Plaited leaf containers** — A lidded box of leaf strips in plain weave, dyed black and red or left natural yellow, whose plaited surface deliberately imitates patterned cloth.

**Motif vocabulary.** Eight-sided star motifs; transverse stripes used as a ground for them; on the plaited box, a surface that mimics cotton textile with supplementary woven gold threads; fringed end-finishes on cloth lengths and blankets.

### Clothing & dress

Dai garments in the collections are women's tube skirts and a jacket. The skirts occur in three material combinations — plain cotton, cotton with silk, and silk alone — which suggests a graded wardrobe from workaday to best, though the catalogue entries do not say so outright; the jacket is cotton. Dress is completed by an embroidered belt made in two parts, of cotton and silk together, the most decorated single garment element recorded. The sources do not describe Dai head coverings, footwear, men's dress or any ceremonial costume distinct from daily wear, and give no vernacular garment names. One point of comparison is recorded: the small Muslim minority known as *Dai Paxi* or *Dai Hui*, descended from Hui merchants from Dali and elsewhere in Yunnan who settled in Xishuangbanna in the early nineteenth century and intermarried locally, wear dress similar to that of their Buddhist neighbours and share their language, customs, rituals and diet — their material culture is described as identical.

### Architecture

Dai villages stand on bamboo plains near rivers or streams. Houses are usually raised on stilts, and some are square in plan. A few are two-storeyed, the upper floor given over to living space and the lower to storage; that lower level is sometimes left without walls altogether, an open undercroft beneath the dwelling. The religious landscape of the village is equally built: until very recently every Dai village had at least one Buddhist temple, and larger villages two to five, these temples also serving as schools where boys sent as novices learned to read and write. Many were destroyed during the Cultural Revolution. Of the older monumental architecture, the sources record only that the twelfth-century Jinghong Golden Hall Kingdom had its capital at Jinghong, and that under the Ming the manorial lords of the region maintained their own armies, prisons and courts. No decorative scheme, roof type or construction detail beyond stilts and bamboo is described.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources name no Dai ceramic or metalworking tradition. What they do document is plant-fibre craft: bamboo work listed among the developed Dai handicrafts, a lidded box plaited from dyed leaf strips, and a model flag of woven and dyed vegetable fibre catalogued as religious or ritual equipment. Bamboo is also a cooking vessel — the fragrant bamboo tube in which glutinous rice is baked. Oil-pressing and winemaking round out the handicraft economy, which since the 1980s has sat alongside tourism revenue in Xishuangbanna following the opening of airports at Jinghong and Mangshi.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not cover Dai jewelry, tattooing or hair practices.

## Music & performance

The sources used — the Wikipedia articles and the museum catalogue records of the objects shown here — contain no account of Dai instruments, song genres or performance occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe any Dai dance or dramatic tradition; the only performance-like practice they record is the mutual pouring of water by young men and women at the New Year, described under Festivals below.

## Festivals & rituals

Dai festivals are mostly religious, and three are named. The **door closing festival** falls on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the Dai calendar, the middle of July in the Gregorian calendar; the **door opening festival** on the fifteenth day of the twelfth Dai month, the middle of October. On both days everyone goes to the Buddhist temple for ritual observance, offering food, flowers and coins to the Buddha. The three months between them are the "closed" season, the most intensely religious part of the year.

The **Water Splashing Festival** is the Dai New Year — glossed as the New Year of June, since it falls in the late sixth or early seventh month of the Dai calendar, the middle of April in the Gregorian calendar, about ten days after Qingming. It is called the most beautiful day of the year and usually lasts three days. At first light villagers go to the temple to wash the figure of the Buddha; after the temple ceremony young men and women pour water over one another, and then move through the settlement in groups sprinkling passers-by as a blessing. The equivalent festival among related Tai-speaking peoples is Songkran.

The central life-cycle rite recorded is monastic: parents commonly sent sons between seven and eighteen to a monastery as novices, where they stayed three years or more learning to read, write and practise the faith before most returned to secular life. Marriage was historically contracted between families of similar social and economic standing, and polygamy was common among chieftains.

## Foodways

Rice is the staple; in the Dehong area it is mainly japonica rice. The best-known Dai snack is **bamboo rice**, glutinous rice packed into a fragrant bamboo tube, soaked in water for about fifteen minutes and then baked over a fire. **Pineapple purple rice** is a second well-known dish. Dai cooking is characterized as raw, fresh, sour and spicy, and the preferences are explained in the sources as dietary reasoning: sour food is held to brighten the eyes, aid digestion and relieve heat, sweet to lift fatigue, and spicy to sharpen the appetite. Sourness is reckoned the finest flavour, and most dishes and snacks are built around it — **sour bamboo shoots** and **sour pork** are the examples given. The subtropical setting supplies the rest of the larder: rice, coffee, rubber, tea, sugar and many kinds of fruit are grown, and winemaking is one of the household crafts. The *Dai Paxi* Muslim minority is recorded as keeping a diet similar to that of Buddhist Dai.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Dai have a substantial written and oral literature: historical documents, legends, stories, poetry, fables and children's stories are described as plentiful. Alongside them stands an astronomical literature — many books on calculating solar and lunar eclipses, most of them written in Dai script — and the Dai calendar itself, which begins in the year 638. The transmission mechanism is the village monastery: because boys were routinely sent to learn reading and writing there, literacy in Dai script among Dai men is reported today to exceed 80 percent. The sources name no single epic or storytelling genre, and do not describe proverb or riddle traditions.

## Language & religion

Dai peoples in China speak Southwestern Tai languages of the Tai–Kadai family: Tai Lü, Tai Nüa (also called Dehong Dai, and identified with Shan), Tai Dam, and Tai Ya or Tai Hongjin; four major varieties are usually distinguished, Tai Lü, Tai Nüa, Tai Rui and Tianxin, the last represented by the dialect of Tianxin in Wuding County. Two further written languages used by the Dai are Tày Pong and Tai Dam. Related Tai–Kadai languages are spoken from Assam to Hainan and Guizhou. The Dai are predominantly Theravada Buddhists, having converted during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries although Buddhism had been present in Yunnan since at least the seventh; earlier animism was not displaced, and belief in natural spirits continues within Dai Buddhism. A small minority are Muslim.
